source.title: Improving Generalization by Controlling Label-Noise Information in Neural Network Weights
source.authors: Hrayr Harutyunyan; Kyle Reing; G. V. Steeg; A. Galstyan

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; text is lightly garbled in some flattened tables and figure labels.
record.tranche_reason: Tests noisy-label memorization and generalization using corrupted-label experiments and a gradient-prediction training method, rather than reproducing the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior findings about fitting random labels and about regularization, but those cited results are not rows. The paper's own Figure 1 comparison and noisy-label experiments are included. Table 1 is flattened; aligned values below are taken from supplementary Tables 4–5.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures noisy-label memorization with and without dropout and weight decay. Its standard-training comparisons bear on V5 independently of the proposed mitigation method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors connect conditional label information in weights to memorization and generalization bounds, and develop gradient-prediction methods that improve noisy-label learning in the tested settings. Superiority is not universal: results depend on the method variant, initialization, dataset, and noise level.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an auxiliary gradient-prediction network and a gradient-norm penalty to limit label information; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with noise type and amount, dataset, training-set size, gradient-prediction distribution, sampling, and whether the auxiliary network is initialized from a cross-entropy model.

fits_no_version.finding: LIMIT suppresses noisy-label memorization and improves clean-test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A training method that restricts label information in predicted gradients can reduce memorization of noisy labels.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The Figure 1 regularization comparison is described in text but its exact training-accuracy values are available only from the plot. The paper does not report a random-label experiment or numerical training-fit results across the corruption sweep. CIFAR-10 experiments report one run per model and dataset pair; uncertainty is bootstrapped over test examples.
record.rows_left_out: No other eligible claim-version results were extracted. The MNIST and CIFAR test-accuracy tables measure clean-test performance across corruption levels but do not establish the full V4 claim because the text does not report matching numeric training-fit results across those conditions. Figure 3 training curves are plotted without a textual claim that training fit remains perfect.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters are not jointly tested.
No true-versus-random-label fitting-time comparison or convergence-time sweep across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and the fully random endpoint are not established. Clean-test degradation across corruption levels is measured.
Complete fitting despite regularization is not established by readable endpoints. Data augmentation is not isolated experimentally, and removing regularization on true labels is not tested.
No separate measurements establish that shared real-label patterns are learned before noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope verdict based solely on an untested part of V5 should be removed. V4's clean-test trends are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing results: for example, MNIST CE accuracy with all training samples falls from 99.2% to 97.2%, 87.2%, and 13.2% as corruption rises from 0% to 50%, 80%, and 89%. These trends alone do not establish the joint perfect-training-fit claim. The supplied figure text does not preserve curves well enough to infer their endpoints or learning order.

versions.untested_parts: No fully random labeling experiment reporting training error and chance test error.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or of convergence time across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

The paper reports clean-test accuracy over some corruption levels, but does not provide extractable numeric training-fit results across the sweep; the plotted training curves do not establish perfect training fit in text.
The paper tests dropout and weight decay under 80% label noise, but does not test removing regularization and measuring generalization on true labels.
No analysis of learning order or comparison of real-label and random-label learning over training.

rows.size_stated: 4 hidden layers, each having 512 ReLU units
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with 80% labels changed to uniformly random incorrect labels; standard regularization comparison in Figure 1.
rows.baseline: 20% training accuracy stated as optimal performance for LIMIT
rows.note: Authors state that non-LIMIT approaches quickly exceed 20% training accuracy by incorporating label-noise information; the plotted value is not given numerically.
rows.check: The text establishes training accuracy above 20%, indicating some noise memorization, but does not establish zero or near-zero training error. The flattened figure supplies no readable endpoint. The 20% reference is expected accuracy from predicting the underlying clean labels, not chance accuracy or a measured control.

rows.operation_detail: LIMIT trained on corrupted MNIST while penalizing label-noise information in gradients.
rows.note: The text calls this optimal training performance on noisy labels; this is the proposed method, not an unregularized baseline.
rows.check: This is the proposed LIMIT method's performance, not a test of the named standard regularizers. The text describes 20% as optimal training performance when avoiding noise memorization; it does not clearly report an exact measured endpoint. Exclude this as a claim-evidence row.

relationships.condition: Failure to prevent some memorization: MNIST with 80% uniformly incorrect labels, dropout 0.5
relationships.reason: Section 2.1 explicitly says the standard approaches exceed 20% training accuracy by incorporating noise information (R2). This supports failure to prevent memorization, but does not establish complete fitting.
relationships.display_finding: With dropout of 0.5, training accuracy exceeded the 20% threshold attainable without memorizing noise, without establishing complete fitting.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: 80% uniform label corruption on MNIST; dropout 0.5, weight decay 0.003, and no regularization
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that the standard approaches quickly exceeded the 20% training-accuracy reference, indicating incorporation of label-noise information (R1–R3). This tests the failure-to-stop-memorization portion of V5.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper does not test the claim's separate assertion about removing regularization and generalizing poorly on true labels; its own comparison is limited to noisy-label training (R1–R4).
